extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers interested in poetics and the theory of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: An Elizabethan-era poetics: definitions, purposes, kinds, and stylistic standards for poetry (poesie), arguing what makes a good poet and poetic work and how poetry compares to history and philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poesy as imitation (mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poesy, therefore, is an art of imitation; for so Aristotle termeth it in the word μίμησις; that is to say, a representing, counterfeiting, or figuring forth: to speak metaphorically, a speaking picture, with this end, to teach and delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sidney cites Aristotle: poetry imitates (represents) reality. The imitation is figurative — a 'speaking picture' — and its twin ends are explicitly pedagogical and pleasurable. Evaluate a poem by how effectively its imitation communicates knowledge or moral truth while also delighting the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: The dual end: to teach and delight
rubrics_metrics.description: Poesy... with this end, to teach and delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet must both instruct (teach virtue, knowledge) and give pleasure (delight), because delight moves people to take up the taught goodness. A poem that instructs without delight will not move readers; a poem that delights without instruction fails its higher purpose. Look for moral or intellectual teaching delivered through pleasurable devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three general kinds of poetic work
rubrics_metrics.description: Of this have been three general kinds: the chief... which they that did imitate the inconceivable excellencies of God; the second kind... of them that deal with matter philosophical; the third, indeed right poets, ... that do merely make to imitate, and imitate both to delight and teach, and delight to move men to take that goodness in hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sidney distinguishes: (1) Divine/scriptural poetry (psalms, sacred songs), (2) Philosophical/ didactic poetry (moral, natural, astronomical, historical treated poetically), and (3) True imaginative poetry that invents 'what may be, and should be.' When assessing, identify which kind the work is and judge it by the standards appropriate to that kind (sacred resonance, correctness of knowledge, or imaginative moral exemplar).

rubrics_metrics.name: True poets imitate what may be and should be
rubrics_metrics.description: These be they, that, as the first and most noble sort, may justly be termed 'vates;' so these are waited on in the excellentest languages and best understandings... to imitate, borrow nothing of what is, hath been, or shall be; but range only, reined with learned discretion, into the divine consideration of what may be, and should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True poetic invention is not mere copying of facts; it creates exemplary, plausible figures/situations that teach by example. Evaluate whether the poet's inventions are believable within their moral logic and whether they illuminate ideals or instructive possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's freedom to surpass nature (making things better than nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the poet, disdaining to be tied to any such subjection, lifted up with the vigour of his own invention, doth grow, in effect, into another nature; in making things either better than nature bringeth forth, or quite anew; forms such as never were in nature...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry is valued for its creative liberty: invention of heightened, idealized, or wholly new forms (heroes, demi-gods, chimeras). Assess the poet's imaginative reach and whether such embellishment serves moral/educational ends rather than mere ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form is secondary: verse is ornament, not essence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not rhyming and versing that maketh a poet... neither is it that feigning notable images of virtues, vices, or what else, with that delightful teaching, which must be the right describing note to know a poet by. Although... the senate of poets have chosen verse as their fittest raiment; meaning, as in matter they passed all in all, so in manner to go beyond them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry may be in prose; versification is a customary garment, not the defining quality. Evaluate works by their imaginative and didactic qualities, not merely by their metre or rhyme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet superior to philosopher and historian (combines precept and example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher... the historian... doth the peerless poet perform both; for whatsoever the philosopher saith should be done, he giveth a perfect picture of it, by some one by whom he pre-supposeth it was done, so as he coupleth the general notion with the particular example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sidney argues the poet uniquely fuses the abstract rule (philosophy) and the concrete example (history). When judging poetry's effectiveness, look for this synthesis: does the poem exemplify general truths through vivid particularization so readers can both grasp and emulate them?

rubrics_metrics.name: Match of mode/genre to matter
rubrics_metrics.description: These be subdivided into sundry more special denominations; the most notable be the heroic, lyric, tragic, comic, satyric, iambic, elegiac, pastoral, and certain others; some of these being termed according to the matter they deal with; some by the sort of verse they like best to write in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and evaluate genre appropriately: heroic for epic material, pastoral for pastoral themes, tragic for high-stakes suffering, etc. The form should fit the subject. Scoring should penalize genre-matter mismatch and reward apt pairing of mode and topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner and diction: measured, proportioned language
rubrics_metrics.description: Not speaking table-talk fashion, or like men in a dream, words as they changeably fall from the mouth, but piecing each syllable of each word by just proportion, according to the dignity of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style must be deliberate and proportionate to subject-matter: careful diction, measured phrasing, and crafted sentences. Anti-patterns: slack, chatty, or slovenly diction; reward careful 'piecing' of language that suits the poem's gravity and aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of figurative devices and 'poetical' ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: His telling of the beasts’ joyfulness, and hills leaping; a heavenly poesy... his prosopopoeias... the often and free changing of persons; his handling his prophecy, which is merely poetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figurative speech (personification, prosopopoeia), vivid imagery, and rhetorical devices are central tools for moving the imagination. Evaluate their appropriateness and effectiveness in producing delight and conveying meaning; avoid devices that are merely flashy without purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's educative and civic function (enriching memory, enabling judgment, enlarging conceit)
rubrics_metrics.description: This purifying of wit, this enriching of memory, enabling of judgment, and enlarging of conceit... the final end is, to lead and draw us to as high a perfection as our degenerate souls... can be capable of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should contribute to the reader's moral and intellectual formation: improving memory, judgment, and imaginative capacity toward virtuous action. When evaluating, consider measurable impact on readers' ethical understanding and imaginative faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical priority and pedagogical utility of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: They that, professing learning, inveigh against poetry, may justly be objected, that they go very near to ungratefulness to seek to deface that which... hath been the first light-giver to ignorance, and first nurse, whose milk by little and little enabled them to feed afterwards of tougher knowledges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sidney claims poetry historically initiates learning and civilizes nations. Assess a work's suitability as an introductory vehicle for complex ideas and its capacity to attract minds to further learning; penalize poetry that closes off curiosity rather than stimulating it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacred poesy as legitimate and high use
rubrics_metrics.description: May not I presume a little farther to show the reasonableness of this word 'vates,' and say, that the holy David’s Psalms are a divine poem?... his handling his prophecy, which is merely poetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sacred or devotional poetry shares poetic devices and can be judged by poetic standards as well as theological ones. When evaluating religious verse, consider its poetic quality alongside reverence, doctrinal fidelity (where relevant), and capacity to console or uplift.
